synopsis: Physical correlation is the prerequisite for trusting virtual collision-mitigation results: models need stated validity domains, representative real-versus-simulated comparisons, correlation bounds and an approved virtual-test envelope before the full scenario matrix is rerun [f4339, f746, f747, f757]. On-road precedents exist, but the corpus reports no published quantitative off-road comparison of simulation-tuned braking thresholds with field results and no independent evidence that virtual or hardware-in-the-loop testing alone covers 100+ off-road site types and all relevant machines and environmental conditions [f153, f154, f5760]. Euro NCAP’s 2026 protocol, version 1.00 dated March 2025, requires physical correlation before prediction submission and random physical verification; at least 75% of verification tests per cluster must meet qualification criteria, although these are on-road requirements [f1215, f1454, f2627]. Planning recommendations distinguish early measurement campaigns on existing machines in 2026–2027 from prototype correlation after arrival in mid-2027, when tests should measure latency, detection range, brake timing, stopping dynamics, repeatability and model error for representative variants [f9375, f744]. Environmental correlation should cover adverse sensor conditions, including measured dust events and dynamic approaches at representative speeds; hardware and mounting must be frozen and correlated before claiming a validated sensor digital twin, and a 2027 sensor change invalidates substantial existing evidence [f5219, f10562, f10658, f11917, f11912]. Expensive integrated tools do not eliminate manufacturer-owned physical correlation, and the programme initially bears both simulation and physical-validation costs; its evidence should explicitly link virtual claims to paired physical tests and pre-declared acceptance bounds [f9318, f10511, f7472, f10207].
